book: 213 - Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About

chapters.relation: Cast as a dialogue with an updated Kant at a tournament, the chapter applies Kant's aesthetics to spectating tennis: it distinguishes free from dependent beauty (a McEnroe drop volley or a Federer stroke judged against the game's history and rules), locates the sublime in a booming ace, a broken record, and the fan's disinterested enthusiasm, and defends aesthetic judgments as disinterested yet subjectively universal. It then turns Kant's ethics onto the court, arguing that calling a line honestly against your own interest has moral worth only when done autonomously, for its own sake, and that gamesmanship like faked injury timeouts seeks an unfair advantage and so is wrong even when within the rules.

chapters.file: ch19 - Stabbing Seles Fans and Fair Play.md
chapters.relation: Opening with Gunther Parche's stabbing of Monica Seles to injure Steffi Graf's rival, the chapter argues that a win-at-all-costs mentality misunderstands sport's value. Using Suits's account of games (lusory goals, means, rules, attitude) and rejecting bare formalism for Simon's broad internalism, it grounds tennis's intrinsic worth in the difficulty of achievement, the level of the opponent, and MacIntyre's notion of a practice with internal goods. It reframes fair play as 'respect for the game,' classifies fans as partisan, purist, or ideally moderate partisan, and concludes that by eliminating Seles, Parche damaged not just her but Graf's legacy and tennis itself because he loved the game too little.

The chapter asks why Anna Kournikova was celebrated as a beauty despite a mediocre record while the far more successful Williams sisters were praised for athleticism, not looks. It uses Plato's Symposium (the ascent from a beautiful body to the Form of Beauty) to show beauty can be more than appearance, then deploys Nussbaum's analysis of objectification (contrasting Playboy's demeaning caption on tennis-player Nicollette Sheridan with Lady Chatterley) and MacKinnon's dominance view to critique the media's commodification of female players. Weaving in commodity racism and bell hooks on black hair, it argues Kournikova's fame reflects a whiteness-privileging color-caste standard of beauty rather than any real athletic or aesthetic superiority.

Starting from Brad Gilbert's 'winning ugly' against McEnroe, the chapter argues that if one can win ugly one can also lose beautifully, and that aesthetic judgment is intrinsic to tennis. It uses Plato's account of techne (craft as true, knowledge-grounded art, versus mere imitation) and Plato's warning against 'lovers of sights and sounds' who stop at appearance rather than reaching Beauty itself, alongside Walton on aesthetic value as pleasurable admiration, to place tennis among the performing arts. It distinguishes physical ugliness (strokes vs. game style, e.g., the retriever) from psychological ugliness (legitimate vs. illegitimate gamesmanship), holding that McEnroe's manipulative rages make a win improper to admire while Federer's full range embodies beautiful play.

chapters.file: ch22 - Arthur Ashe Philosopher in Motion.md
chapters.relation: Inverting Clark Graebner's claim that Ashe's 'loose' play expressed his race, the chapter mines Arthur Ashe's life to test theories of race. It rejects racialism, then argues both major constructivisms fail: Charles Mills's materialist Racial Contract faces an 'assignment problem' because the privileged, successful Ashe eludes the material burdens that supposedly define blackness (Billie Jean King's 'I'm blacker than Arthur'), while Du Bois's narrative constructivism faces an 'authenticity problem' shown by South African students calling Ashe an Uncle Tom and his anguish over his daughter's white doll. Ashe's antiapartheid 'trade' in playing Johannesburg and his disciplined-yet-reckless character model a 'looseness' that treats race as a set of justice and identity projects, not a metaphysical thing.

chapters.file: ch23 - The Ridiculous Meets the Radical in the Battle of the Sexes.md
chapters.relation: Comparing Jackie Robinson's somber dignity with the comic spectacle of Billie Jean King's 1973 Battle of the Sexes against Bobby Riggs, the chapter asks why sexism could be joked about as theater while racism demanded gravity, arguing race operates in a competitive male-vs-male public sphere whereas sexism is intimate and domestic. It reads King's victory through Maria Lugones's feminist notions of 'playful world-traveling' and 'loving perception': where Margaret Court stayed rigid and lost, King playfully entered Riggs's circus, matched his showmanship, and ultimately made the match about tennis. King's later affection for Riggs illustrates loving perception, recasting the event as a shared act of social transformation rather than a simple good-versus-evil win.

The chapter uses Aristotle's three friendships (pleasure, usefulness, virtue) to ask how tennis rivals competing for one prize can be friends, illustrating pleasure with Borg and Gerulaitis, usefulness with the tense but genuine Ashe-McEnroe Davis Cup bond, and virtue with the Evert-Navratilova rivalry that grew into deep mutual care despite a competitive women's tour. It adds C. S. Lewis's view that friends stand side by side absorbed in a shared thing, then reads Jimmy Connors as a Nietzschean Ubermensch whose master-morality drive to dominate makes him, paradoxically, the best 'star friend' by pushing rivals to their limits. It closes unresolved on whether the tension between friendship and rivalry can ever be eliminated.

holes.name: Playful World-Traveling and Loving Perception
holes.what: Maria Lugones's feminist idea that oppressed people resist injustice by playfully 'traveling' into others' worlds and adopting a loving, non-arrogant perception that sees them as fellow subjects.
holes.why: Chapter 23's entire analysis of how Billie Jean King beat Riggs and later loved him is built on Lugones's world-traveling and loving perception, and no taxonomy philosopher or concept captures Lugones.
